frontend.prompt:
Implement the UI and client-side request handling so that "other users'" resources are shown read-only and users cannot attempt to modify them. Follow these concrete rules and tests; do not assume new server endpoints or fields exist without coordinating with backend if missing.

Required runtime assumptions (must be verified with backend):
- Each resource GET response MUST include an owner identifier field (name may vary; commonly owner_id). If the current API does not expose an owner identifier in resource responses, coordinate with backend to add it.
- The frontend has a reliable way to get the current user's id (and whether the current user is a superuser). If not present, coordinate with backend to expose a /me endpoint or include current user id in the authentication token payload.

UI behaviour (exact):
1) Determining ownership:
   - Consider a resource "ownedByCurrentUser" when resource.owner_id === currentUser.id.
   - All other cases are treated as "other user's resource".

2) Read vs write affordances:
   - If ownedByCurrentUser === true: show normal edit/save/delete controls (write allowed).
   - If ownedByCurrentUser === false: always render the resource form/view as read-only (disable editable inputs) and hide or disable edit/save/delete controls.
   - Do not show an alternate "request access" control unless product explicitly requires it (do not invent new flows).

3) Superuser behaviour in the UI:
   - If currentUser.is_superuser === true and ownedByCurrentUser === false: treat the resource as read-only in the UI (same as above). Do not enable edit/delete controls for superuser on others' resources.
   - If currentUser.is_superuser === true and ownedByCurrentUser === true: allow full editing.

4) Create (POST) UI constraints:
   - When creating a resource, do not render or send an owner_id field. The frontend MUST NOT allow the user to select or set owner_id. The backend will set owner_id server-side to the creating user.

5) Error handling / responses mapping (exact user-visible flows):
   - If an API GET returns 404: show a "Not found" page or message. Treat it as the resource not existing.
   - If an API PUT or DELETE returns 403 with response body { "detail": "Read-only access" }: show a clear non-editable message such as "Read-only access: you cannot modify this item." Keep the view read-only and do not retry the write automatically.
   - If an API PUT, PATCH or DELETE returns 404 for the current user: show "Not found" (do not display a permissions error) — this covers the case where normal users attempt to access others' resources and the backend intentionally returns 404.
   - For other status codes, surface appropriate generic messages per existing app patterns.

6) Defensive client behavior:
   - Do not rely solely on UI controls to prevent writes. Always handle 403/{"detail":"Read-only access"} and 404 responses gracefully as described.
   - When an edit attempt results in 403 with detail "Read-only access", log the event and present the exact message to users.

Acceptance tests to implement in the frontend test-suite:
- Case A (superuser viewing other user's resource): GET returns resource with owner_id != currentUser.id and currentUser.is_superuser true -> UI shows resource in read-only mode; edit/delete controls hidden/disabled.
- Case B (superuser attempts direct edit): simulate PUT/DELETE to resource owned by another user -> server returns 403 {"detail":"Read-only access"} -> UI shows the exact read-only message and remains read-only.
- Case C (normal user viewing other user's resource): GET returns 404 -> UI shows Not Found.
- Case D (creating a resource): client sends POST without owner_id -> on successful create, verify created resource is owned by the current user (owner_id equals currentUser.id in subsequent GET), and UI treats it as editable for the creator.

Developer notes:
- Do not modify or forge owner_id in POST/PUT payloads. Always omit owner_id on create and do not change owner_id on updates.
- If the frontend previously relied on a backend-provided field that is not available, open a clear ticket to backend to include owner_id and/or a current-user endpoint; do not proceed by guessing a different field name.

backend.prompt:
Implement server-side permission and ownership enforcement to satisfy the stated constraints. The behavior must be explicit, deterministic, and covered by tests. Do not assume endpoint paths or field names beyond the following abstract contract points — implement the rules against your existing resource endpoints and representations.

Contract and exact behaviors to implement:
1) Read (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS):
   - Any authenticated user (including superuser and normal user) may GET an existing resource. If the resource exists, return it (200 with the resource payload). If the resource does not exist, return 404.
   - For regular users requesting another user's resource, do NOT return 403; if the resource does not exist for them by policy, return 404 (see rule 3). However, per requirement, superusers may read others' resources, so GET for an existing resource should succeed for superusers.

2) Write (PUT, PATCH) and Delete (DELETE):
   - If the requesting user is the owner of the resource (resource.owner_id equals request.user.id), allow the operation and return the usual success status per your API conventions (e.g., 200/204). No special body is required other than normal success semantics.
   - If the requesting user is a superuser and the resource is owned by another user: deny the write operation with an HTTP 403 response. The response body MUST be JSON with exactly { "detail": "Read-only access" } and Content-Type application/json. Do not return 404 in this case — the requirement explicitly requires 403 with that detail for superuser write attempts on others' resources.
   - If the requesting user is NOT the owner and NOT a superuser (a normal user attempting to access another user's resource): do NOT reveal the resource; return 404.

3) Non-existent resources:
   - Any operation (GET/PUT/DELETE etc.) against a resource id that does not exist must return 404.

4) Create (POST):
   - When creating a resource, ignore owner_id sent by the client. The server MUST set resource.owner_id (or equivalent owner field) to the current authenticated user's id. Ensure owner assignment occurs in server-side creation logic (not just client validation).

5) Implementation guidance (pattern):
   - Centralize this logic in a permission check or middleware-layer so all resource-modifying endpoints share the same behavior.
   - Pseudocode permission logic for a request touching resource R and user U:
     - If resource R does not exist: return 404.
     - If request.method in SAFE_METHODS (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS): return allow.
     - Else (method is PUT/PATCH/DELETE):
         - If R.owner_id == U.id: allow.
         - Else if U.is_superuser: return 403, body { "detail": "Read-only access" }.
         - Else: return 404.
   - On POST: set R.owner_id = U.id before saving; ignore incoming owner_id from client payload.

6) Response details (must be exact where specified):
   - For superuser write attempts on others' resources: status 403, body exactly { "detail": "Read-only access" } (JSON). Use UTF-8 and Content-Type: application/json.
   - For normal users accessing others' resources: return 404 (no special body required beyond existing 404 format).
   - For non-existent resources: return 404.

7) Tests to add (unit/integration):
   - Superuser GET other user's existing resource -> 200 and resource payload present.
   - Superuser PUT/DELETE other user's resource -> 403 with body { "detail": "Read-only access" } and Content-Type application/json.
   - Normal user GET other user's resource -> 404.
   - Any user (superuser or normal) requesting a non-existent resource -> 404.
   - POST create: client-sent owner_id ignored; created resource.owner_id == request.user.id.
   - Owner editing/deleting own resource -> allowed and returns normal success codes.

8) Backwards-compatibility/coordination notes:
   - If frontend needs owner_id in GET responses or a current-user endpoint, add this to the API contract. If that is not already present, coordinate a minimal change: include owner_id in resource representation and/or expose current user info; do not assume it exists.

Developer implementation hints (do not treat these as requirements if they conflict with your stack):
- If using a framework with permission classes/middleware (e.g., Django REST Framework, Express middleware), implement this logic in a reusable permission middleware/class and attach it to resource endpoints.
- Ensure tests assert response body equality for the 403 case (the detail string must match exactly: "Read-only access").
- Log permission denials for audit, but avoid leaking resource existence to unauthorized normal users (return 404 for them).

Do not change other unrelated authorization rules. If any field names (owner_id, is_superuser) differ in your codebase, map them directly but keep the exact behaviors and response text required above.
